digest.intro: Energy infrastructure wars, AI's invisible workforce, and hardware that plays Doom.

items.title: Mapping AI Colonialism, Block by Block
items.blurb: Brown senior Cunyan Ma built an interactive map connecting tech companies — through their intermediaries — to the data workers in the Global South whose annotation labor makes AI function. Most of what's known about this workforce comes from scattered journalism; this is the first attempt to aggregate databases, original collection, and news reports into a single visible geography. Ma frames it explicitly as 'AI colonialism made spatial' — and the map is freely available online.

items.title: The Safety Discourse Is Optimizing for the Wrong Disaster
items.blurb: The piece makes a clean structural argument: industry-backed AI safety legislation targets catastrophic edge cases — the Hollywood scenarios — while the slow diffuse damage (dependency, cognitive atrophy, engineered envy) accrues unreported. A teenager with an unhealthy AI companion never appears in a lawsuit. A student who outsources all thinking to a chatbot doesn't make headlines. The bar 'doesn't encourage suicide' is technically clearable while a product still corrodes how an entire generation thinks.

items.title: 60 Years of Cellular Aging, Reversed in One Conversion
items.blurb: University of Bonn researchers converted blood cells from an 80-year-old directly into neural stem cells — and the resulting cells showed molecular age markers under 20. The key detail: they bypassed induced pluripotency entirely, going cell-type to cell-type, which appears to carry the de-aging effect through the transition. Published in peer-reviewed Aging Cell; early-stage, not a therapy, but the mechanistic finding about what reprogramming does to the aging clock is genuinely novel.

items.title: Switzerland at 1:1 Scale, One Block Per Meter
items.blurb: Someone rendered the entire country of Switzerland in Minecraft-style voxels at true 1:1 scale from SwissTopo open geodata — every block is one meter, the Matterhorn is exactly as tall and steep as the real one, and glaciers, lakes, forests, and dam walls are all present. A slider overlays the actual Swiss aerial photograph. The Jungfrau-Aletsch UNESCO region (2,400 km²) is free; the full country costs 15 CHF. It's territory-as-medium: the most literal possible collapse of cartography and fabrication logic into a single navigable object.

items.title: The $40 Synth That Became a Community Firmware Playground
items.blurb: The M-Vave FM-1 launched as a cheap pocket FM synthesizer; by July, Reddit's r/synthdiy had reverse-engineered its firmware; by September, custom builds were shipping; by October, M-Vave responded not with a cease-and-desist but by open-sourcing the whole thing under GPLv3 and releasing an SDK with a browser-based workbench. There are now more community firmware projects than anyone can track — and yes, it plays Doom. It's a rare case of a hardware company leaning into the hack instead of killing it.

facts.fact: Blood cells from an 80-year-old were converted into neural stem cells with biological age markers resembling those of a person under 20 — without passing through a pluripotent intermediate state.
The entire country of Switzerland has been rendered in Minecraft voxels at true 1:1 scale from open government geodata — every block is exactly one meter, including glacier geometry and dam walls.
M-Vave responded to community reverse-engineering of the FM-1 synth not with a patch to block it, but by releasing the full application source code under GPLv3 and publishing an official SDK.

A Brown University undergraduate built the first geographic map linking AI companies through intermediaries to their Global South data workers — most prior knowledge of this workforce came only from individual journalism pieces.

art_picks.title: Mauvais Sang
art_picks.creator: Leos Carax
art_picks.why: Carax builds a film that runs entirely on surface-as-system — color, gesture, music, and bodies in space as a kind of generative language. Denis Lavant's long sprint through a Paris night to David Bowie is one of cinema's great moments of pure expressive force; the rest of the film earns it.

art_picks.title: UUmwelt
art_picks.creator: Pierre Huyghe
art_picks.why: Huyghe partnered with neuroscientists in Kyoto, had a subject imagine images while an fMRI scanned their brain activity, then let a neural network generate thousands of visual reconstructions from that data — hallucinatory, unstable mental images installed across MoMA's Sculpture Garden. It's the feedback loop between cognition, biology, and machine vision made physically inhabitable.

art_picks.title: re:member
art_picks.creator: Ólafur Arnalds
art_picks.why: Arnalds built a custom software system that triggers two self-playing pianos in response to what he plays live — a feedback loop where the room, the machines, and the human become one instrument. The album documents that system; hearing it live at Town Hall this week is the real thing.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, 11 West 53rd Street, Manhattan
events.why: Freestanding screens throughout MoMA's outdoor sculpture garden generate hallucinatory, shifting images in real time from fMRI brain-scan data and machine learning — the installation responds to visitor presence via sensors, making the space itself a living cognitive system before it closes November 29.

events.name: Synthesize Me: Olga Titus & Michael Dickey
events.why: A two-person show pairing artists whose work sits exactly at the edge where material and process collapse into each other — the kind of tightly focused gallery exhibition that rewards close looking over spectacle.

events.name: EJ Hauser: Sun Water Sky
events.why: Hauser's paintings feel like systems that almost resolve — color and form pressing against legibility without ever quite becoming landscape or abstraction; the kind of quiet obsessive studio work that makes you want to go back to whatever you're building.

events.name: Ólafur Arnalds — Two Nights at The Town Hall
events.venue: The Town Hall, 123 West 43rd Street, Manhattan
events.why: Two intimate nights (1,500-seat historic venue) from the Icelandic composer whose live show is built around generative software and self-playing pianos — a rare case where the system IS the performance.

events.name: Salon Art + Design — 15th Edition
events.venue: Park Avenue Armory, 643 Park Avenue, Manhattan
events.why: 50+ international galleries filling the Armory's 55,000-sq-ft Drill Hall with collectible design, furniture, ceramics, lighting, and 20th-century art — the rare fair where a 1970s Italian chair and a postwar painting share a booth and neither feels out of place.
